content:
Doc purpose
- Capture security/compliance review notes for the Shadow Traffic (“Shadow Evals”) feature.
- Focus areas: data classification, logging policy, retention defaults, access controls, audit requirements, and customer controls.
- This is a working doc; decisions below should be reflected in the restricted Confluence policy update before Beta/GA.

Meeting context
- Dates: 2025-10-29 (initial review), 2025-11-06 (follow-up on judge scoring + telemetry), 2025-11-14 (post-beta tightening after capacity spike incident)
- Facilitator: Naomi Feldman (Security/Compliance)
- Eng points of contact:
  - Platform/Policy: Ethan Park, Benji Okafor
  - Telemetry: Logan Wright, Nadia Rahman, Caleb Johnson
  - Console/Rollouts: Dylan Brooks, Chloe Martin, Jada Williams
  - Applied ML/Evals: Jonas Weber, Olivia Grant
  - SRE: Sean Gallagher, Rafael Mendes
  - Security Eng: Marcus Lin (implementation), Kevin Osei (audit/retention controls)

In-scope data flows (what we’re reviewing)
1) Primary request received (normal inference path)
2) Shadow sampler (policy-controlled) mirrors subset of requests to one or more shadow targets
3) Shadow execution is async and must never block/alter the primary response
4) Shadow outputs + derived eval signals are emitted to telemetry pipeline
5) Aggregations power Console dashboard and rollout quality gates
6) (Optional) payload samples retained for debugging / judge calibration, behind restricted access and explicit customer controls

Key security principle (repeated): “Shadow Evals must be safe-by-default.”
- Default posture: collect minimal necessary data, retain briefly, aggressively redact, restrict access, and prevent surprise cross-region replication.
- The feature must remain usable even when customers disable payload storage.

Data classification (proposed)
We should tag each data element explicitly in the schema and treat storage differently by default.

A) Customer content (high risk)
- Prompt text / messages (user-provided)
- Tool call arguments and tool outputs (may include PII/secrets)
- Model outputs (may include PII if present in prompt or generated)
Classification: “Restricted / Customer Content”
Default: DO NOT store raw content for shadow runs unless explicitly enabled by customer + contract tier allows.

B) Derived signals (medium risk)
- Judge scores (win-rate, preference, rubric sub-scores)
- Format adherence booleans (e.g., valid JSON, schema match)
- Safety policy outcomes (pass/fail categories; avoid storing full text triggers)
- Similarity metrics (embedding distance / n-gram overlap) computed from outputs
Classification: “Confidential / Telemetry”
Default: store (aggregated), allow limited raw event storage for short retention.

C) Operational metadata (medium/low risk, but high cardinality risk)
- request_id (Redwood-generated)
- route_id / deployment / region
- model identifiers (primary + shadow target model/version/quant profile)
- latency metrics, token counts, batch size, cache hit
- sampling policy id and whether shadow run executed or dropped
Classification: “Confidential / Operational”
Default: store; ensure request_id is not customer-provided; avoid storing customer user identifiers.

D) Customer identifiers (contractual/PII adjacent)
- customer_id, workspace/project id
- (Potentially) end_user_id if customer passes one
Classification: “Confidential / Customer Account Data”
Default: store customer_id; treat end_user_id as sensitive: either do not ingest, or only ingest as a one-way HMAC (see notes below).

Explicit non-goal: We are not building a general “prompt logging” product under Shadow Evals.

Logging policy decisions (draft)
1) No raw prompts/outputs in standard logs
- Shadow runner application logs must not include prompt text or model output text.
- Logs may include: request_id, route_id, customer_id, shadow_target_id, error codes, timeouts, queue drop reason.
- Exception: Security-approved “restricted payload sample” pipeline (separate store, short-lived, gated access).

2) Telemetry event payloads must be tiered
- “shadow_eval.run_event” (raw-ish event) should be configurable to include/exclude content fields.
- Default configuration: content fields absent; only derived signals + operational metadata.

3) Strict redaction before any storage
- If any content is stored (opt-in), run redaction filters prior to persistence.
- Redaction must happen before writing to: telemetry sink, debug sample store, and any replay queues.
- Minimum redaction filters (v1): emails, phone numbers, SSNs, credit cards, API keys/common secret patterns.
- Known limitation: redaction is heuristic; must be positioned as “best effort” and not a guarantee.

4) No cross-customer training use
- Shadow Evals data is for customer’s evaluation and Redwood operational reliability only.
- Any “model improvement / training” use is out of scope and requires separate product + contractual language.

Retention defaults (draft proposal)
We need defaults that satisfy:
- fast debugging during Beta
- SOC2 expectations on minimizing retention
- customer control, especially for regulated workloads

Proposed retention tiers (subject to PM-613 pricing/packaging but we should set security minimums):
A) Aggregated metrics tables (recommended default)
- Contents: counts, rates, percentiles, mean judge score, win-rate deltas; grouped by coarse dimensions (route/model/region/time bucket)
- Retention: 30 days default; configurable up to 90 days for enterprise tiers
- Residency: stored in-region if customer is on Private/VPC; for Hosted, store in chosen region cluster (no global replication beyond DR policy)

B) Raw shadow run events (no prompt/output text by default)
- Contents: request_id, route_id, customer_id, target identifiers, latency/token metrics, judge scores, safety outcomes
- Retention: 7 days default; configurable down to 24h; up to 14 days for enterprise
- Access: internal only; customer-visible only via aggregated views in Console

C) Restricted payload samples (opt-in only)
- Contents: redacted prompt/output snippets OR fully redacted payload (depending on mode)
- Purpose: debugging, judge calibration, incident root cause analysis
- Retention: 72 hours default; configurable down to 0 (disabled) or up to 7 days with explicit approval
- Storage: separate bucket/table with stricter IAM + break-glass process
- Access: requires ticket + approval (INT-3321 pattern), scoped to on-call/Security/Evals as needed

D) Judge prompts and judge model outputs
- Judge prompt templates (static): keep as code/config (normal retention)
- Judge model raw outputs: treat as derived signals; do not store judge chain-of-thought; store normalized scores + short rationale only if needed
- Retention: align with Raw shadow run events (7–14 days)

Data residency notes
- Shadow execution must occur in the same region as the primary request unless explicitly configured otherwise (default: same-region).
- Telemetry storage for raw events should be region-scoped; avoid centralizing raw events across regions.
- If customers are in “EU-only” posture, ensure the shadow targets are EU-only compatible and the judge model execution (if hosted by Redwood) is also EU.
- Console global views should query aggregated tables, not copy raw events into a centralized store.

Access controls (internal)
1) Role-based access
- Default: engineers do not have access to raw event payload samples.
- Access tiers:
  - Tier 0: Aggregated dashboard access (most employees with relevant product access)
  - Tier 1: Raw events (no content) for Telemetry/SRE with production support role
  - Tier 2: Restricted payload samples (content) only via approved group + time-bound access

2) Break-glass and time-bounded grants
- Use time-limited grants for Tier 2 (hours/days).
- Require justification (incident id / customer escalation) and manager + Security approval.
- Log every access (who/when/what query).

3) Separation of duties
- Applied ML should not have blanket access to customer content across accounts.
- Any judge calibration requiring content should be done with:
  - customer-provided sample sets, or
  - restricted samples for a single allowlisted customer with explicit opt-in.

Audit logging requirements
- For any system storing raw events or payload samples:
  - Record read access (principal, source IP / device posture if available, timestamp, dataset/table, query hash)
  - Record write access (pipeline identity, schema version)
  - Record export actions (download to local, transfer to external)
- For Admin controls:
  - Log toggles of: global kill switch, per-route shadow enable, sampling %, retention mode changes
  - Retain audit logs for 1 year minimum (SOC2 alignment) even if payload retention is short
- Note: audit logs must not include prompt/output text.

Customer controls (product requirements from Security)
- Per-customer master switch: shadow traffic OFF by default for existing accounts; ON only when customer enables.
- Per-route enable + sampling percentage with safe defaults (e.g., 0% default, max default cap).
- Customer allowlist for which routes can store payload samples (if any).
- Retention configurability: allow customer to set raw event retention to minimal (24h) or off (0) where supported.
- Data export: aggregated metrics export OK; raw payload export should require explicit customer action and be scoped.
- Opt-out of judge scoring if judge execution would violate customer policy (e.g., certain regulated data types).

Identity / identifiers (avoid leaking customer identifiers)
- request_id must be generated by Redwood and not incorporate customer-provided identifiers.
- If customers provide end_user_id:
  - Do not store plaintext end_user_id.
  - If needed for per-user bucketing, store HMAC(end_user_id, customer-scoped secret) to prevent cross-customer correlation.
- Avoid storing IP addresses in shadow eval event schema; if needed for abuse/security, store coarse geo/ASN at most.

Threat model notes (abbreviated)
Risks we discussed:
- Accidental content logging due to debug statements / exception traces
- Over-collection (prompt/output stored without customer intent)
- Cross-region replication violating residency commitments
- Unauthorized internal access to payload samples
- Metric tags causing sensitive leakage (e.g., tool name includes user email)
- Shadow execution acting as an unintended data exfil path (e.g., shadow target routed to wrong environment)
- Prompt injection affecting judge model (judge prompt reveals internal policies or produces unsafe outputs that get stored)

Mitigations mapped:
- Linting + CI checks for “no content in logs” patterns (add to redwood/pr-48288 follow-up)
- Hard schema separation between events-with-content vs events-without-content
- Policy engine validation: shadow target must match customer residency + environment
- Restricted sample store with tight IAM + audit logging + break-glass
- Tag allowlists + bucketing to prevent sensitive tags (ties to ENG-2435)
- Judge prompt hardening: do not include secrets; store only normalized scores; never store chain-of-thought

Decisions / agreements (as of 2025-11-14)
- Default behavior for Beta: no prompt/output storage; only derived signals + operational metadata.
- Payload sample mode is enterprise opt-in + explicit per-customer allowlist + 72h default retention.
- All access to payload samples is ticketed and audited (INT-3321 workflow).
- Same-region execution is default and required for EU-only customers.
- No judge chain-of-thought stored; store scores and (optional) short rationale capped to N chars with redaction.

Open questions
- Do we need a customer-facing DPA addendum specifically naming Shadow Evals data categories, or can we cover under existing “service telemetry” language?
- Judge execution location: for Hosted, do we always run judge in the same region, or can we run judge in a dedicated “eval region”? (Security recommendation: same region by default; any cross-region needs explicit customer toggle.)
- Should we allow customers to bring their own judge model endpoint (BYO judge) to avoid Redwood handling sensitive content? (would reduce risk but adds complexity)
- For Private/on-prem: where do we store aggregated metrics (customer-managed DB vs Redwood-managed)? Need clarity for GA.

Action items
- Marcus Lin: add explicit log-scrubbing tests + a “content logging ban” static check for shadow runner codepaths (target: before Beta enablement).
- Kevin Osei: define audit log schema for admin toggles + dataset access logs; ensure 1y retention independent of payload retention.
- Logan Wright / Caleb Johnson: split telemetry events into two topics (content-free default vs restricted samples) and enforce schema validation.
- Nadia Rahman: confirm billing/metering does not require prompt/output capture; ensure cost attribution uses token counts only.
- Dylan Brooks / Marissa Cole: add Console UI language that clearly states what is and is not stored by default; add customer toggles for retention/sample storage.
- Ethan Park / Benji Okafor: policy validation for residency + env; ensure shadow targets cannot point to a different compliance boundary by mistake.
- Jonas Weber / Olivia Grant: judge prompt guidelines update: no chain-of-thought storage; rationale length cap; prompt injection considerations.
- Sean Gallagher / Rafael Mendes: runbook additions: when kill switch is used, confirm payload sample pipeline is also stopped; add verification queries.

Notes from 2025-11-14 follow-up (post capacity spike learnings)
- Incident reinforced that “operational guardrails” are also a privacy control: overload can cause engineers to turn on verbose logging.
- Agreed: no emergency debug logging that prints prompts/outputs; instead, rely on restricted sample pipeline with approvals.
- Add explicit ‘drop_reason’ metrics to avoid needing raw content for debugging (queue_full, budget_exceeded, policy_disabled, timeout, target_unavailable).

Checklist for Beta readiness (security)
- [ ] Default retention settings implemented and verified in prod config
- [ ] Restricted payload sample store disabled by default; enable requires allowlist + approvals
- [ ] Audit logs for admin toggles implemented
- [ ] IAM groups + time-bound access process documented (link INT-3321)
- [ ] Residency validation tests pass (EU-only accounts)
- [ ] Redaction filters integrated and validated on sample payloads
- [ ] Console copy reviewed (no misleading claims)

Owner notes (Naomi)
- We should keep this feature positioned as “evaluation telemetry” not “logging.” Customers will ask if we store prompts. Answer must be consistent: default is no; opt-in is tightly controlled; retention is short; access is audited.
- Ensure contracts and SOC2 narratives explicitly mention: minimal collection, least privilege, audit trails, and customer controls for retention/residency.
